evidence.quote:
The study recorded 125 boiling curves and CHF values on nominally
identical bare copper surfaces, establishing an average boiling curve and mean CHF value.

The pool boiling tests were carried
out with double-distilled water under saturated conditions at atmo­
spheric pressure, representing the most common conditions used in
literature.

Each boiling curve was recorded until CHF, after which the car­
tridge heaters were turned off and the sample was left to cool down
before initiating the next run.

The manufacturing process for bare copper samples (electrolytic
purity, >99.9 % Cu) with 14 mm diameter involved a three-step pro­
cedure: (1) sanding the surface, (2) cleaning the surface, and (3) gluing
and mounting the sample.

The sample being tested was then mounted onto a copper block and
fixed with an insulative PEEK holder.

In this study, a total of 125 experimental runs were conducted to
measure the pool boiling performance of 25 bare copper samples.

When recording a boiling curve, the heat flux was increased at a rate of
less than 0.2 kW m-2 s-1 during the natural convection regime and at a
rate of less than 2 kW m-2 s-1 during nucleate boiling.

All measurements were performed at atmospheric pressure
under saturated conditions using double-distilled water.

The glass boiling chamber with an inner diameter of 60 mm was filled
with 200 mL of water.

A total of 25 bare copper surfaces were
prepared and tested in nominally identical way, i.e., by sanding and
subsequent cleaning, with five boiling curves recorded on each surface
up to the CHF incipience

The bare copper
surfaces before boiling exhibited only tool marks from abrasive sand­
paper treatment, and the same case was observed for the bare copper
surfaces after boiling tests.
